title: transient-metrics-void-and-pager-surge-postmortem
content:
Executive summary:

On 2025-01-12 between ~02:07 and 03:18 UTC we experienced a transient wholesale loss of several Prometheus-derived metrics (ingest and runtime histograms) that triggered an alert storm and an apparent SLO burn for the hosted-api service. The underlying production service was healthy; customer-facing latency and error rates did not materially change. The alerting noise originated from metric ingestion backpressure and a cascading consumer restart pattern in the ingest pipeline, which led to metric gaps and abrupt SLI drops.

Impact:
- Number of incidents paged: 8 oncall pages over ~70 minutes.
- Services paged: hosted-api (alerts for request_latency_p50/p95 histograms), routing (kv-cache hit-rate drop alerts), telemetry-ingest (consumer lag increase).
- External user impact: none observed (no increase in 5xx; no customer tickets).
- Internal impact: ~90 minutes of distracted oncall time, delayed low-priority tasks, one rush rollback of a non-related config by a different team.

Detection timeline (UTC):
- 02:07: first alert: hosted-api_request_latency_p95_slo_burn (60s window) fired (alert rule based on histogram cutover).
- 02:10: multiple downstream histogram metrics sparse / NaN observed in the dashboard.
- 02:18: telemetry-ingest consumer group kinesis-consumer-3 restarted repeatedly (observed via logs).
- 02:23: oncall triage: Lina confirmed absence of corresponding increase in error-rate or latency in the request logs.
- 02:35: mitigation: temporary alert muting applied for the affected SLOs to stop paging while we investigate (note: muting rule ID: mute-2025-01-12-01).
- 02:40: discovered that metric-forwarder (v2.8.1) memory spike correlated with a GC stall; container OOMs back-to-back caused ingestion backlog.
- 02:52: restarted metric-forwarder with controlled concurrency and bumped JVM flags (Xmx -> 3g).
- 03:05: consumer-3 restarted stabilized; queue lag returned to normal by 03:12.
- 03:18: dashboards show metric recovery and synthetic heartbeat counters resumed.

Root cause hypothesis (confirmed by logs + heap dumps):
1) A low-rate but high-cardinality trace path (feature-flagged metrics from a new A/B experiment) increased cardinality of the histogram buckets and elevated memory pressure in metric-forwarder.
2) metric-forwarder (Java-based wrapper) hit a full GC pause pattern due to a previously unknown object retention path in histogram aggregation logic.
3) During GC stalls the forwarder stopped shipping metrics, causing consumer lag and repeated restarts of telemetry-ingest. The consumer restarts and backlog produced a temporary metric void that downstream SLO rules interpreted as zeros or NaN and fired burn alerts.

Why alerts amplified:
- Several SLO alert rules assume continuous ingestion and use short windows (30–60s) with no NaN handling logic; missing series equate to low SLI values.
- Alert grouping and deduplication rules were insufficient for histogram-derived alerts: each percentile rule produced its own page.
- No synthetic heartbeat metric existed on the ingest cluster to differentiate true service outages from ingestion gaps.

Immediate mitigations performed:
- Applied alert mute window for the affected SLO rules and pinned the mute to the telemetry-ingest ownership channel to avoid accidental long-term silence.
- Restarted metric-forwarder with reduced aggregation concurrency and increased heap.
- Added quick-rate-limit for the new A/B experiment metrics at the source (feature flag owner: product/experiment-team) to prevent further cardinality spikes.
- Stabilized consumer group by forcing a controlled rebalance and setting a slower restart backoff.

Short-term action items (triage owners in parentheses):
- (SRE) Revert any recent non-critical metric client changes in the next deploy window.
- (Telemetry) Add a temporary synthetic heartbeat gauge emitted by forwarder every 30s, and create an alert that fires only if heartbeat missing for >2m.
- (SRE) Add NaN/series-missing handling to SLO rules: change rule semantics so missing series do not equate to 0% SLI (use last-known or synthetic heartbeat).
- (Product) Disable the A/B experiment metric emission until cardinality is reduced (owner: Priya Nair).
- (SRE/Platform) Increase forwarder memory limit on the telemetry cluster from 2g -> 4g for the short term and monitor GC metrics.

Long-term remediation proposals:
- Replace Java-based aggregation in metric-forwarder with a streaming C++/Rust path that has lower pause characteristics (proposal: SRE-arch-2025-02).
- Implement ingestion-side cardinality caps and automatic sampling for high-cardinality labels before aggregation.
- Standardize SLO alert rules to be resilient to short ingestion gaps: incorporate heartbeat checks and use percentile continuity windows.
- Alerting platform change: enable multi-metric grouping for histogram alerts to avoid N pages for N percentiles.
- Create an oncall playbook: "Metrics-Ingest-Transient-Failure" runbook with step-by-step checks (consumer lag, forwarder GC, container OOM, synthetic heartbeat).

Runbook draft (KEY STEPS):
1) When you see histogram percentiles drop or SLO burn but no user-visible error increase: check synthetic heartbeat (if absent, assume ingestion gap).
2) Look at telemetry-ingest consumer lag and forwarder pod GC/heap metrics (grafana links in linked artifacts).
3) If forwarder OOM/GC: scale memory + restart one pod at a time; apply short concurrency throttle.
4) If queue backlog: enforce consumer backoff and controlled rebalance; avoid mass restarts.
5) If caused by new metric emission: contact experiment owner and temporarily disable metric emission.
6) Apply a temporary mute for the alert group and annotate the incident with mute ID.
7) After stabilization, run a small verification load (synthetic) to confirm metrics flow for 5–10 minutes before unmuting alerts.

Oncall play-by-play notes (raw):
- Arjun: noticed p95 spike and immediately checked request logs — no matching latency. Suspected telemetry.
- Lina: grepped forwarder logs -> GC "Full GC paused" repeated. Started heap dump capture.
- Samir: created temporary mute (mute-2025-01-12-01), informed SRE channel and product-experiment owner.
- Priya: acknowledged experiment and pushed temporary flag to stop emitting the high-cardinality labels.
- Maya: adjusted forwarder JVM flags and restarted pods sequentially.

Post-incident metrics to track (owners):
- forwarder_heap_usage_max (SRE)
- forwarder_gc_pause_ms_95 (SRE)
- telemetry_ingest_consumer_lag (Telemetry)
- synthetic_heartbeat_present (SRE/Tel)
- slo_alert_paging_count_weekly (SRE/Oncall)

Lessons learned / notes:
- Histogram and percentile-based SLOs are fragile when the ingestion layer is not assumed to be 100% reliable. We need explicit patterns for missing data.
- Short alert windows are good for latency-sensitive regressions but require defensiveness against ingestion gaps.
- Product experiments can accidentally create observability churn; feature flags should gate metric emission until a cardinality review is passed.
- Mutes must be scoped and annotated. The temporary mute prevented cognitive overload but required manual oversight to avoid missing real incidents.

Open questions / follow-ups:
- Do we adopt last-known-value semantics for missing series across all SLO rules, or only for histograms? (Proposal: only histograms for now.)
- How quickly can telemetry team prototype a low-pause aggregator in Rust? (Estimate required).
- What sampling/backpressure knobs should be exposed to product teams to avoid future surprises?

Next steps (owners + ETA):
- Telemetry to ship synthetic heartbeat + heartbeat alert (owner: Samir) — ETA: 2025-01-20.
- SRE to update SLO alert rules with NaN handling and grouping (owner: Maya) — ETA: 2025-01-22.
- Product/Experiment team to freeze metric emission for the flagged experiment and run a cardinality audit (owner: Priya) — ETA: 2025-01-15.
- Architecture review for forwarder rewrite (owner: Arjun) — schedule by 2025-02-01.

Appendix (useful snippets):
- quick checks: kubectl logs -n telemetry forwarder-<pod> | grep "Full GC"
- heap dump location: s3://redwood-dumps/forwarder/2025-01-12/heapdump-<pod>.hprof
- mute ID: mute-2025-01-12-01
- Jira: SRE-4192 (forwarder GC investigation); SRE-4193 (runbook: Metrics-Ingest-Transient-Failure); TELE-221 (heartbeat alert)

Document history:
- 2025-01-12 Maya Chen: initial notes and timeline.
- 2025-01-13 Lina Gomez: added heap dump analysis and mitigation steps.
- 2025-01-14 Arjun Rao: added long-term remediation proposals and runbook draft.

Notes to reviewers:
- This is a working postmortem; please add missing facts, link to additional logs, and propose different prioritizations if you disagree. The immediate priority is to ship heartbeat and change SLO rule behavior to avoid repeat pages.
